Car Guy Got 1969 Charger R/T Hemi 4-Speed After Watching Bullitt in 1975, He Loves Driving It Still
67 photos
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile
Dodge made three grand debuts for the legendary Charger: once in 1966, on January 1, the second time on September 14, 1967, and the third on October 17, 1968. The first time was the absolute premiere for the moniker, the second saw the introduction of the revered second generation, and the third was the first public screening of “Bullitt.”
Say what you will, but those ten minutes and fifty-three seconds it starred alongside Steve McQueen were the best advertising spot the Charger enjoyed before or since. You need proof of that? Typical shelf life of a TV spot in the late sixties hovered between six months to a year. “Bullitt” kept the Charger evergreen to 2026, but as far as its commercial success went, the movie sold a second-gen Charger a full nineteen years after its debut.
In 1975, Bob Dyrda was a college senior, and dreamt about muscle ccars. Fatefully, he watched a television rerun of the classic blockbuster “Bullitt,” and he enthusiastically noted, "I settled on the Charger and that was all it took." For the following twelve years, he diligently saved his penny and he saved his dime, for he knew there would be a time when he would buy a brand-new 426.
Sorry for not going through with the Beach Boys theme song, but Bob’s Charger couldn’t have come with the legendary Chevy big-block. Instead, the gearhead had to settle for a Chrysler offer, so he got an old drag racer second-gen Dodge Charger with a big ol’ orange engine under the hood. One that matched its name with the sobriquet of the paint used on that very block. 426 Hemi, in Hemi Orange.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile Yup. The man has a Hemi Charger. Need I say more? How about a pair of 4s? 4-speed, 4.10 Dana 60. And 46,006 miles. Or, to be accurate, that’s how many it had in late June 2026, when Lou Costabile asked the owner out for a shootout. For YouTube. The result is embedded below.
The owner is probably a strong manifester, because he bought an original 1969 Dodge Charger brochure before acquiring his actual unicorn. Yes, Bullitt’s bad guys rode in a ’68 R/T, but Bob liked the taillight of the ’69 better. THE TAILLIGHTS! The man is clearly a strong-willed gearhead with non-mainstream tastes. Everyone is head over (w)heels with the signature round lamps of the ’68, and he casually says “No, thanks. I’ll take the better-looking ones.”
The ’69 is clearly a fan’s favorite for the signature feature found at the opposite end of the back lights – namely, the split grille that made TV screen waves in the Dukes of Hazzard series. To each their own. Besides, Bob doesn’t really get to see how he looks like driving his 4-speeed Hemi Charger from the outside, mainly because he’s in the car – and loving every nanosecond of it.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile So, after he got the original brochure and patiently waited to turn his ultimate high-octane dream into a fantastic reality, Bob found the perfect car. The story took a romantic turn in 1987 while discussing marriage with his future girlfriend Maryanne.
She supported his automotive passion, wisely advising, "Well if you really want this car why don't you get it before we get married otherwise life will probably take us away from it." Bob placed an ad in Hemmings Motor News, eventually flying out to New York to buy this modified drag racer for 8,500 dollars.
The dream-come-true new owner struck gold by finding two original factory broadcast sheets and the fender tag, confirming the car is a true “Y14” Sold Car ordered strictly for racing. Built with a 426 Hemi engine and a 4-speed manual transmission with a Hurst shifter, it features the A34 Super Track Pak. In Dodge parlance, that’s the Dana 60 rear axle with 4.10 gears, a 26-inch radiator, and power front disc brakes.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile Stripped of extra weight, the car was ordered as a radio-delete model, featuring only a remote driver mirror and a locking gas cap as options. Bob purchased this brute in 1987 from Dave Schwarz in Massapequa, New York, who had bought it in 1986 from a man named Ed in Bay Shore. A handwritten sheet passed down from owner to owner also mysteriously mentioned a connection with a certain Joe Garity. You’ll understand the reason and rhyme behind this list of random names if you watch the video.
Because the engine underwent extensive modifications at Bob Sharp Racing in Danbury, Connecticut, Bob Dyrda suspects the car originally lived there. Supporting this theory, he discovered a vintage Connecticut license plate reading hidden underneath the back seat cushion. A July 1971 renewal sticker completely covered a previous 1970 sticker, strongly suggesting the vehicle belonged to a Connecticut resident from 1969 until it was likely sold to a second owner around 1971.
The handwritten notes detailed a serious high-performance engine rebuild. The already unhinged (but hotter than the hot hinges of you-know-what) motor was balanced, blueprinted, ported, and polished, receiving new 12.5:1 compression pistons, a Crower camshaft, and upgraded valvetrain components.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile The original Carter carburetors were swapped for a pair of Carter Competition 750 CFM carburetors, while the factory dual-breaker distributor was replaced by a Mallory electronic ignition system and high-performance spark plug wires to extract every drop of performance from the power stroke.
Serious racers spare no expense, and this vehicle received Hooker headers to replace the cast iron exhaust manifolds. A separate Ford starter solenoid was installed on the inner fender to accommodate those massive headers. Furthermore, the 4-speed transmission was significantly beefed-up using Fairbanks performance components.
When Bob bought the car, it wore unidentified aftermarket wheels, but the previous owner kept them, allowing selling the car to Bob with standard Chrysler stamped steelies.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile The exterior wore a fresh coat of factory-correct red paint, but the iconic white R/T tail stripe had been removed, leaving only faint remnants under the trunk lid. To save the last ounce of weight and morph this muscle car into a sleeper, previous owners removed both door emblems and the front bumper guards.
In the engine bay, a misaligned driver hood hinge caused a stress crack in the subframe, which was later repaired with a small welded metal patch. Inside the cabin, the front seat headrests were removed, and the factory wood-grained shifter knob was replaced by a Hurst T-handle. Although originally a radio-delete car, someone added a Chrysler AM radio featuring a 1968 faceplate, routing it to a broken fender antenna.
Scratches on the steering column suggest an aftermarket tachometer was previously mounted there. Under the hood, an incorrect power drum brake master cylinder had replaced the original unit. In the 39 years since he’s owned it (bought in October, 1987), Bob Dyrda took the car back to as close to factory as possible, and today he prides himself in driving one of the best-looking Hemi Chargers of the second-gen era. He even built a website for it , specifically to find out more of its history.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile The Charger R/T moniker debuted in 1968, with Dodge building 475 Hemi cars. This limited production run consisted of 211 units equipped with 4-speed manual transmissions, while the remaining 264 vehicles received the heavy-duty three-speed automatic gearboxes.
For the legendary 1969 model year, Dodge assembled 432 Charger R/T Hemis. Out of those, 207 examples featured the highly desirable 4-speed manual transmission, and 225 came with automatics. By 1970, soaring insurance premiums effectively killed the muscle car market, causing production to plummet dramatically. Only 112 buyers stepped up for the ultimate engine option that year, perfectly split between 56 manual cars and 56 automatic vehicles.
The legendary big-block engine made its final appearance in 1971, with only 63 Charger R/Ts leaving the assembly line. That final batch included 30 manual transmission cars and 33 automatics. Across those 4 glorious production years, Dodge manufactured a grand total of just 1,082 Charger R/T Hemi vehicles.
Looking at the broader picture, the factory produced 53,195 Dodge Charger R/T models across all engine options during that memorable era, with the peak coming right in 1969, at 19,298 cars. All in all, the Charger R/T Hemi saw a grand total of 1,173 cars made between 1968 and 1971, of which 498 had three pedals and a big iron stick in the middle of the floor pan between the front passengers.
